newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-THE PURGE IS ON BUT INCOMPLETE - BY ING BARINGS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-THE PURGE IS ON BUT INCOMPLETE - BY ING BARINGS.

text.p: In its November report titled "The Purge is on but
Incomplete," securities firm ING Barings warns that Indian stock exchanges have yet to discount grim news on the political, economic and corporate fronts.
The month of October has been a turbulent one for the market, we predicted in the last issue of the India Market Monitor.

The Sensex is practically unchanged (3239.94 on 29 October against 3239.48 on 30 September!) despite violent intra-day and day-on-day moves of about 100 points, on a third of the trading days in October.

On the political front, the stalemate resulting from the hung assembly in Uttar Pradesh continues, while the BJP has lost control of the Gujarat government to expelled dissident leader Shankarsingh Waghela.

The UP imbroglio and the scams in Bihar have also put the United Front government in a tight spot. The Congress has had a change of guard with Sitaram Kesri taking over as president of the party from P.V. Narasimha Rao, who has been chargesheeted in several cases.
All political parties are currently facing rought weather and the central government appears to be less keen to press on with important economic reforms.
On the corporate front, corporate governance is in the news.
ITC is in the dock for serious FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulations Act) violations and five other prominent business houses are alleged to have bribed the former petroleum minister.
The corporate world is nervous with investigating agencies continuing to raid business houses and arrest top executives.
The stock market is currently drifting listlessly, searching desperately for direction. We believe the market has yet to complete the downward correction prior to forming a long-term bottom.

This is borne out of the belief that the market has not fully appreciated the grim realities on the political, economic and corporate fronts. We continue to hold a contrarian view on this subject as shown in the following table:

It should be noted that the major areas where we differ from the consensus are on the issues of recessionary trends witnessed in the economy and the pain of liberalisation which the Indian industry has escaped so far.
We are noting early signals of the exhaustion demand for consumer as well as industrial goods on the back of robust consumption in the last three-four years.
The primary reason for demand fatigue is the small consumer base of the fragile Indian economy, thanks to the uneven distribution of income.

The gradient of the income pyramid is rising due to the lack of a percolation effect. This leads to short cycles of rapid demand growth (three-four years) which exhausts pent-up demand, followed by a demand lull (one-two years).

We have witnessed two such cycles in the last ten years: the first during Rajiv Gandhi's era and now in the Narasimha Rao era of liberalisation. The following are the early signals of recessionary trends:
** Growth rate of industrial production heading downward since 2Q96;
** Falling import/export growth since 2Q96;
** Dismal excise/customs collection;
** Growing deposits/falling advances by banks;
** Rising inventories/receivables;
** Impending production cuts;
** Idling freight capacity
Another major factor not discounted by the capital market is the pain of liberalisation. No country has escaped this when embarking on the path of opening up and globalising its economy.

The first spell of liberalisation under Rajiv Gandhi's leadership witnessed import-led economic growth, culminating in the balance-of-payment crisis. The second era of liberalisation under Narasimha Rao stripped the insulated Indian industries of all protection and encouraged the creation of massive fresh capacities in all sectors.

The pain of economic reforms undertaken by Rao was delayed due to the higher degree of protection in the early 1990s (which progressively came down), robust international commodity prices (which have since crashed) and an unprecedented boom in the capital markets (which have now sunk to abysmally low levels).
We believe the change in the business environment and the emergence of recessionary trends will hasten the shake-out of Indian businesses in the next two years.

We also feel that the attendant industrial unrest will heighten the need for a retrenchment policy and labour reforms. However, India's pain during this transition need not be characterised by hyper-inflation (as in Latin American countries) or rapidly shrinking income (as in Russia/East European nations).
We think India's peaceful economic reforms programme will lead to restructuring of businesses after a long-drawn shakeout.

During the last three years foreign institutional investors have banked upon the robust economic performance and phenomenal corporate earnings growth in India and invested substantial funds without any returns.

We believe the market is going to form a long-term bottom as it recognises recessionary trends and evaporating corporate earnings growth. After this period of disenchantment, we see a good upside for the Indian stock market later in 1997.

In the meanwhile, we continue to advise investors to restructure their portfolios to overweight PSEs and underweight private sector businesses. On the sectoral front, we recommend investors to BUY oil, refineries, telecom, banks, utilities and petrochemicals and SELL automobiles, cement and steel companies.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
